shelves.name: In Her Own Voice
shelves.staffNote: Women writing their own wanting — a Greek island, a Montana boarding house, a madhouse cell. They sit on the shelves below as well; this is where they are gathered.

shelves.name: Letters
shelves.staffNote: Real people, writing to the person they wanted, without expecting to be read by us. Nothing in the library is closer to the bone.

shelves.name: Read in One Sitting
shelves.staffNote: Poems, fragments and short letters — the whole thing in the time you have. Gathered from the shelves below rather than taken off them.

shelves.name: Longing & Restraint
shelves.staffNote: Desire as pressure rather than release. The shelf most readers start on, and the one they come back to.

shelves.name: Gothic & Uncanny
shelves.staffNote: Danger and appetite braided together. Historically the shelf that performs best here.

shelves.name: Sapphic
shelves.staffNote: Women writing women, from before there was a word for it that anyone wanted to use.

shelves.name: Fantasy & Fable
shelves.staffNote: Invented worlds, where the rules about appetite were always looser than at home.

shelves.name: Devotional
shelves.staffNote: Frank about the body and unembarrassed by it. The oldest tradition in the library.

shelves.name: Bawdy & Comic
shelves.staffNote: Sex as comedy, told by people enjoying the telling. The oldest joke in European literature, and the women are in on it.

passages.text: Sometimes after an hour of apathy, my strange and beautiful companion would take my hand and hold it with a fond pressure, renewed again and again; blushing softly, gazing in my face with languid and burning eyes, and breathing so fast that her dress rose and fell with the tumultuous respiration. It was like the ardor of a lover; it embarrassed me; it was hateful and yet over-powering; and with gloating eyes she drew me to her, and her hot lips traveled along my cheek in kisses; and she would whisper, almost in sobs, “You are mine, you _shall_ be mine, you and I are one for ever.” Then she had thrown herself back in her chair, with her small hands over her eyes, leaving me trembling.

I took her hand as I spoke. I was a little shy, as lonely people are, but the situation made me eloquent, and even bold. She pressed my hand, she laid hers upon it, and her eyes glowed, as, looking hastily into mine, she smiled again, and blushed.

His hair—the color of hers—waved back from his temples in the same way as before. His skin was not more burned than it had been at Grand Isle. She found in his eyes, when he looked at her for one silent moment, the same tender caress, with an added warmth and entreaty which had not been there before—the same glance which had penetrated to the sleeping places of her soul and awakened them.

She touched him with her finger-tips, she kissed his throat, his wrists, the palms of his hands, his eyelids, his hair. Strange, subtle kisses, unlike the kisses of women. And often, between her purrings, she murmured love-words in some strange fierce language of her own, brushing his ears and his eyes with her lips the while.

For one second before she left the room their eyes met, she raised a red rose, which she had taken from the silver vase, casually to her lips, and then passed out, but Paul knew she had meant the kiss for him, and his whole being was uplifted.

Silently, patiently, he was recoiling away from her even now. It was the stillness, and the timeless sort of patience, in a man impatient and passionate, that touched Connie's womb. She saw it in his bent head, the quick, quiet hands, the crouching of his slender, sensitive loins; something patient and withdrawn. She felt his experience had been deeper and wider than her own; much deeper and wider, and perhaps more deadly. And this relieved her of herself; she felt almost irresponsible.

Suddenly Wanda looked at me so strangely that my senses became confused and passion swept over my head like a conflagration. Losing command over myself, I threw my arms about her and clung to her lips, and she—she drew me close to her heaving breast.

She came to me, seated herself on my knees with lightning-like rapidity, threw her arms around my neck, clasped her hands behind my head, and her mouth clung to mine in a fierce embrace; I felt her breast, half-uncovered, throbbing against mine, and her interlaced fingers moving convulsively in my hair. A shudder ran all over my body and the nipples of my bosom stood erect.

They confined their evolutions to a small space: they intermingled like waves. Soon they formed in couples, and without interrupting the step, unfastened their girdles and let their pink tunics glide to the ground. An odour of naked women spread about the men, dominating the perfume of the flowers and the steam of the gaping viands. They threw themselves backwards with brusque movements, with their bellies tightly drawn, and their arms over their eyes. When a lover coming home late at night kisses his beloved, who is asleep or in bed, in order to show her his desire, it is called a "kiss that awakens." On such an occasion the woman may pretend to be asleep at the time of her lover's arrival, so that she may know his intention and obtain respect from him.

Auddalika says, "Females do not emit as males do. The males simply remove their desire, while the females, from their consciousness of desire, feel a certain kind of pleasure, which gives them satisfaction, but it is impossible for them to tell you what kind of pleasure they feel. The fact from which this becomes evident is, that males, when engaged in coition, cease of themselves after emission, and are satisfied, but it is not so with females."

When one of them takes both the lips of the other between his or her own, it is called "a clasping kiss." A woman, however, only takes this kind of kiss from a man who has no moustache. And on the occasion of this kiss, if one of them touches the teeth, the tongue, and the palate of the other, with his or her tongue, it is called the "fighting of the tongue." In the same way, the pressing of the teeth of the one against the mouth of the other is to be practised.

When two who are mated in every respect burn with the fire of the innumerable forces within them, which set their bodies longing towards each other with the desire to inter-penetrate and to encompass one another, the fusion of joy and rapture is not purely physical. The half swooning sense of flux which overtakes the spirit in that eternal moment at the apex of rapture sweeps into its flaming tides the whole essence of the man and woman, and as it were, the heat of the contact vapourises their consciousness so that it fills the whole of cosmic space. For the moment they are identified with the divine thoughts, the waves of eternal force, which to the Mystic often appear in terms of golden light.

She cried 'Laura,' up the garden,
'Did you miss me?
Come and kiss me.
Never mind my bruises,
Hug me, kiss me, suck my juices
Squeezed from goblin fruits for you,
Goblin pulp and goblin dew.
Eat me, drink me, love me;
Laura, make much of me:
For your sake I have braved the glen
And had to do with goblin merchant men.'

Laura started from her chair,
Flung her arms up in the air,
Clutched her hair:
'Lizzie, Lizzie, have you tasted
For my sake the fruit forbidden?
Must your light like mine be hidden,
Your young life like mine be wasted,
Undone in mine undoing,
And ruined in my ruin,
Thirsty, cankered, goblin-ridden?'--
She clung about her sister,
Kissed and kissed and kissed her:
Tears once again
Refreshed her shrunken eyes,
Dropping like rain
After long sultry drouth;
Shaking with aguish fear, and pain,
She kissed and kissed her with a hungry mouth.

She sang the heart out of his breast,
The words out of his tongue;
Hand and foot and pulse he paused
Till her song was sung.
Then he spoke up from his place
Simple words and true:
'Scanty goods have I to give,
Scanty skill to woo;
But I have a will to work,
And a heart for you:
Bid me stay or bid me go.'

A red rose peeping through a white?
Or else a cherry, double grac'd,
Within a lily centre plac'd?
Or ever mark'd the pretty beam
A strawberry shows half-drown'd in cream?
Or seen rich rubies blushing through

So like to this, nay all the rest,

My dear Husband (for the last time I use that title!), shall I never see you again? Shall I never have the pleasure of embracing you before death? What dost thou say, wretched Heloise? Dost thou know what thou desirest? Couldst thou behold those brilliant eyes without recalling the tender glances which have been so fatal to thee? Couldst thou see that majestic air of Abelard without being jealous of everyone who beholds so attractive a man? That mouth cannot be looked upon without desire; in short, no woman can view the person of Abelard without danger. Ask no more therefore to see Abelard; if the memory of him has caused thee so much trouble, Heloise, what would not his presence do? What desires will it not excite in thy soul? How will it be possible to keep thy reason at the sight of so lovable a man?

I shall follow you with my eyes over the Heath. Will you come towards evening instead of before dinner? When you are gone, ’tis past—if you do not come till the evening I have something to look forward to all day. Come round to my window for a moment when you have read this. Thank your Mother, for the preserves, for me. The raspberry will be too sweet not having any acid; therefore as you are so good a girl I shall make you a present of it. Good bye

My greatest torment since I have known you has been the fear of you being a little inclined to the Cressid; but that suspicion I dismiss utterly and remain happy in the surety of your Love, which I assure you is as much a wonder to me as a delight. Send me the words ‘Good night’ to put under my pillow.

works.title: Carmilla
works.author: Sheridan Le Fanu
works.blurb: A lonely castle in Styria, a guest who arrives by accident, and a friendship that neither girl can quite name. Written twenty-six years before Dracula, and far stranger about desire than anything that followed it.
contentNotes: Predatory intimacy, presented as such
A death in the family, early

works.title: Vathek
works.author: William Beckford
works.blurb: A caliph with an appetite for everything forbidden walks knowingly toward damnation. Beckford wrote it in French at twenty-one, reportedly in a single sitting, and it has been embarrassing respectable readers ever since.
contentNotes: Cruelty played for style
Human sacrifice, in the manner of an oriental tale

works.title: The Awakening
works.author: Kate Chopin
works.blurb: A summer on Grand Isle, and a woman who discovers she is a person rather than a wife. It ended Chopin's career and is now the novel everyone else was writing toward.
contentNotes: Marital estrangement
Suicide

works.title: Three Weeks
works.author: Elinor Glyn
works.blurb: A young Englishman and an older woman who is nobody's idea of a heroine. The scandal of 1907, written by a woman, and the reason a tiger-skin rug became a joke your grandmother would have understood.
contentNotes: Adultery
A violent death offstage

works.title: Lady Chatterley's Lover
works.author: D. H. Lawrence
works.blurb: The most famous banned book in English, in the unexpurgated text Lawrence had privately printed in Florence. Explicit, tender, and much angrier about class than its reputation suggests.
contentNotes: Explicit throughout
Disability written from the outside
Period language about class

works.title: The Well of Loneliness
works.author: Radclyffe Hall
works.blurb: Tried for obscenity in 1928 for a single line asking that two women be left in peace. A long, serious, unhappy novel that a great many women read in secret for forty years.
contentNotes: Period sexology and its language
Sustained loneliness; an unhappy ending

works.title: Venus in Furs
works.author: Leopold von Sacher-Masoch
works.blurb: A man asks a woman to own him, and she makes him sign for it. Female dominance negotiated in writing, a century before anyone had the vocabulary — and much stranger and funnier than its reputation.
contentNotes: Consensual submission, contractually agreed
Period attitudes to servants and to race

works.title: Mademoiselle de Maupin
works.author: Théophile Gautier
works.blurb: A young man falls for a beautiful youth who is a woman in disguise, and she for the woman he loves. Gautier's preface — the best defence of art without moral purpose in French — comes attached, unrepentant.
contentNotes: Desire between women, and gender disguise throughout
A long preface arguing for art without moral purpose

works.title: Aphrodite
works.author: Pierre Louÿs
works.blurb: Alexandria, and a courtesan who asks three impossible things of the man who wants her. Louÿs wrote the ancient world as a place where appetite was ordinary and the consequences were not.
contentNotes: Explicit throughout
A crucifixion, and a death by exposure
Slavery in ancient Alexandria, presented as ordinary

works.title: The Kama Sutra
works.author: Vatsyayana
works.blurb: Systematic, unembarrassed and far more interested in women's pleasure than anything written in Europe for the next fifteen hundred years. Much stranger and more practical than its reputation.
contentNotes: Explicit and systematic
Chapters on procurement and on other men's wives, as period documents
Period attitudes to caste and to consent

works.title: Ars Amatoria
works.author: Ovid
works.blurb: The seduction manual that got its author exiled to the Black Sea. Witty, worldly, and written by someone who plainly liked women's company as well as their bodies.
contentNotes: One passage advises force; noted rather than excised
Period attitudes to women

works.title: The Decameron
works.author: Giovanni Boccaccio
works.blurb: Ten young people flee the plague and tell a hundred tales to pass the time — about lust, appetite, hypocrisy and the getting round of husbands. Payne's is the English that was never bowdlerised.
contentNotes: Explicit and comic throughout
Some tales turn on a trick played on a woman; the tellers argue the morals
Period attitudes to class and to the clergy

works.title: The Heptameron
works.author: Marguerite de Navarre
works.blurb: A queen's own collection, and the only one of its date where women argue the meaning of every story after it is told — often disagreeing with the men, usually winning.
contentNotes: Several tales concern coercion, and the tellers debate it openly
Period religious framing

works.title: Droll Stories
works.author: Honoré de Balzac
works.blurb: Balzac writing Rabelais: monks, wives, and the getting of what everyone wants. Deliberately mock-medieval, entirely filthy, and much funnier than the century that produced it.
contentNotes: Bawdy comedy, sometimes at a woman's expense
Deliberately mock-archaic English

works.title: The Song of Songs
works.author: Anonymous
works.blurb: Three thousand years old and still the frankest love poetry in the Western canon — two voices, mostly hers, wanting each other in a garden. It survived into scripture on the argument that it was an allegory. Read it and see whether you believe that.
contentNotes: Desire, plainly stated, and mutual
A brief scene of violence against the woman by the city watchmen

works.title: Married Love
works.author: Marie Stopes
works.blurb: The book that told women their own desire had a rhythm and was not a fault. Banned in America, outsold almost everything in Britain, and the clearest answer to what this library is for.
contentNotes: Period eugenic language in one chapter
Medical advice a century out of date

works.title: Sappho
works.author: Sappho
works.blurb: Everything of hers that survived: one complete poem, and a hundred or so fragments — several of them a single line, quoted by some grammarian to settle a point about a verb. Wharton's plain 1885 prose, lifted out of the scholarly apparatus it was printed inside.
contentNotes: Fragmentary by nature; many pieces break off mid-line
Desire for women, plainly
Wedding songs, some of them at the bridegroom's expense

works.title: Goblin Market
works.author: Christina Rossetti
works.blurb: Two sisters, a fruit market only one of them can see, and the most physical poem in Victorian English about tasting what you were told not to. Twenty-one poems chosen out of the collected Rossetti — the strand of it that is about wanting.
contentNotes: A stated selection from the 1862 and 1866 volumes, not the complete poems
The goblins force the fruit on the sister who refuses them
One long poem argues renunciation and does not settle it

works.title: Maria; or, The Wrongs of Woman
works.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
works.blurb: A woman shut in a madhouse by a husband who owns her property, her child and her testimony. Wollstonecraft died before she finished it, and Godwin printed what there was — so the book breaks off still arguing, among her notes toward the endings she was choosing between.
contentNotes: Unfinished; it ends in the author's own notes
Rape, a pressed abortion and prostitution, in the warder's account
Confinement, and a child taken

works.title: Wuthering Heights
works.author: Emily Brontë
works.blurb: Reviewed on publication as coarse and disagreeable, which was fair. It is still the most sustained account in English of wanting one particular person long past the point where it does anybody any good.
contentNotes: Violence to people, animals and children, at length
A marriage obtained by imprisonment
Period language about race and about class

works.title: The Story of Mary MacLane
works.author: Mary MacLane
works.blurb: Three months of diary by a nineteen-year-old in Butte, Montana who wanted fame, a good dinner, the Devil, and a woman she calls the anemone lady — and printed all of it. It sold a hundred thousand copies in a month, and Butte's own library refused to stock it.
contentNotes: Written at nineteen, about her own body throughout
Desire for an older woman, named and never retracted
Sustained talk of death, and of wanting the Devil to come for her

works.title: Keynotes
works.author: George Egerton
works.blurb: Eight stories about what women think when nobody is asking, written by Mary Chavelita Dunne under a man's name. Punch was parodying it inside a year. The husbands in them are not villains; they are simply not listening.
contentNotes: Marital discontent and infidelity, unpunished
A childbirth, and a servant's dead child
Period attitudes to drink and to service

works.title: His Hour
works.author: Elinor Glyn
works.blurb: Glyn again, three years after Three Weeks, written at the request of the Dowager Empress of Russia and dedicated to her. A widow, a Cossack prince who will not be refused, and a night in a snowbound hut that she spends with a pistol held to her own head.
contentNotes: He engineers her ruin to force the marriage, and the book knows it
A long stretch in which she is furious and he is not sorry
Period attitudes to Russia, and to servants

works.title: The Age of Innocence
works.author: Edith Wharton
works.blurb: The first Pulitzer given to a woman, and a novel in which the two people it is about touch almost never. Restraint as the subject rather than the limit: old New York closes around them so politely that nobody ever has to say anything aloud.
contentNotes: Adultery, considered at length and largely not acted upon
Period attitudes to divorce, and to women's money

works.title: Short and Explicit
works.author: Donne, Herrick, Behn, Dickinson
works.blurb: Twenty-one poems, none longer than a few minutes: Donne talking a woman out of her clothes, Herrick dreaming he is a vine, Aphra Behn writing the female answer to the whole tradition, and Dickinson in four lines saying more than any of them. Chosen and set together here.
contentNotes: An anthology assembled for this library, from four public-domain editions
Explicit in places, and seventeenth-century about it
Behn's *The Disappointment* turns on a woman saying stop and not being heard; the poem is on her side

works.title: Short and Explicit II
works.author: Behn, Wilcox, Lowell, Teasdale, Millay
works.blurb: Seventeen poems by six women, 1680 to 1923: Aphra Behn demanding to know where desire has been all her life, the poem that made Ella Wheeler Wilcox a scandal, Amy Lowell stripping a lover like an almond, and Millay — born a woman and distressed — declining to call it love in the morning. Chosen and set together here.
contentNotes: An anthology assembled for this library, from seven public-domain editions
Frank rather than graphic — warmer than the first volume, and less explicit
*Patterns* ends with a death in war

works.title: The Love Letters of Abelard and Heloise
works.author: Heloise and Peter Abelard
works.blurb: She was his student, then his wife, then an abbess who would not say she was sorry. Written after her uncle's men had castrated him and both were shut in religious houses — and she is still arguing, at length, that what they did was worth it.
contentNotes: Five letters: three are hers, two are his
Castration, referred to throughout
A forced separation, and vows taken under pressure
Twelfth-century theology about women, argued back at

works.title: Letters to Gilbert Imlay
works.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
works.blurb: Seventy-seven letters to the American speculator who fathered her child and would not stay. The woman who wrote the Vindication, in love and then in humiliation, writing it all down as it happened — and *Maria* is what she made of it afterwards.
contentNotes: Two suicide attempts, one of them the subject of a letter
A pregnancy, and a man's absence through it
Published by her husband the year she died

works.title: Letters to Fanny Brawne
works.author: John Keats
works.blurb: Thirty-seven letters written between his first haemorrhage and the last boat to Italy, to the girl next door he could not marry. Jealous, ashamed of being jealous, and completely without defences — which is why they were considered unpublishable for fifty years.
contentNotes: Tuberculosis, and a young man's knowledge of it
Jealousy and possessiveness, admitted as such
He died at twenty-five; the letters stop rather than end
